facts.text: The European goldfinch has a red face with black markings around the eyes, a black-and-white head and a broad yellow bar on its black wings.
facts.quote: The breeding male has a red face with black markings around the eyes, and a black-and-white head.

facts.text: It is a small finch, 12–13 cm long, with a wingspan of 21–25 cm and a weight of 14 to 19 g.
facts.quote: The average European goldfinch is 12–13 cm (4.7–5.1 in) long, has a wingspan of 21–25 cm (8.3–9.8 in) and weighs 14 to 19 g (0.49 to 0.67 oz).

facts.text: Its song is a pleasant silvery twittering, and its call is a melodic tickeLIT.
facts.quote: The song can be described as a pleasant silvery twittering. The call is a melodic tickeLIT, and the song is a tinkling medley of trills and twitters

facts.text: The female builds the neat, compact nest entirely herself, generally completing it within a week, while the male accompanies her but does not contribute.
facts.quote: The female builds the nest entirely herself, generally completing it within a week. The male accompanies her, but does not contribute.

facts.text: The nest is attached to twigs with spider silk and lined with plant down such as that from thistles.
facts.quote: It is made of moss and lichen and is lined with plant down, such as that from thistles. It is attached to the twigs of the tree with spider silk.

facts.text: Its preferred food is small seeds from thistles, cornflowers and teasels, though it also eats insects when feeding its young.
facts.quote: The European goldfinch's preferred food is small seeds such as beige-coloured sunflower hearts and those from thistles (the Latin name is from Carduus, a genus of thistles), cornflowers, and teasels, but it also eats insects when it feeds its young.

facts.text: It uses its tweezerlike bill to extract hard-to-get seeds, and one goldfinch in Armenia ate 30 seeds from a sunflower head in a single hour.
facts.quote: One European Goldfinch in Armenia ate 30 seeds from a sunflower head in a single hour.

facts.text: The word 'goldfinch' first appeared in English in the 14th century, used by Geoffrey Chaucer in his unfinished The Cook's Tale.
facts.quote: The English word 'goldfinch' was first used in the second half of the 14th century by Geoffrey Chaucer in his unfinished The Cook's Tale: "Gaillard he was as goldfynch in the shawe (Gaily dressed he was as is a goldfinch in the woods)".
